text: Elsie Tu CBE GBM (née Hume; Chinese: 杜葉錫恩; 2 June 1913 – 8 December 2015), formerly known as Elsie Elliott, was a British-born Hong Kong social activist who served as an elected member of the Urban Council of Hong Kong from 1963 to 1995 and a member of the Legislative Council of Hong Kong from 1988 to 1995. Born on 2 June 1913 in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, into a working-class family of John and Florence Hume, she was the second of four children. After attending Benwell Secondary Girls' School and Heaton Secondary School, she studied at Armstrong College, graduating in 1937 with a Bachelor of Arts. From 1937 to 1947, she worked as a schoolteacher in Halifax, where she volunteered in Civil Defence during the Second World War. She converted to Christianity in 1932 during her university years. In 1946, she married William Elliott and moved to China in 1947 as a missionary with the Christian Missions in Many Lands, stationed in Yifeng. After the Chinese Communist Party took power in 1949 and expelled foreign missionaries from mainland China, she relocated to Hong Kong, living in an illegal apartment in the Wong Tai Sin squatter community known as Kai Tak New Village, where she observed corruption involving triad protection money. Disillusioned with her husband's rigid Protestant faith and the Plymouth Brethren's refusal to engage in social issues, she left the church in 1955 and divorced him in 1964. She lived briefly in a kitchen in a Kowloon Walled City tenement and founded Mu Kuang English School in 1954 in an old army tent near Kai Tak, starting with 30 pupils; she remained principal until 2000. The school now serves 1,300 children in low-income families on Kung Lok Road in Kwun Tong. She met Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei at the school, who became her husband 30 years later. Elliott was shocked by the injustices in Hong Kong, including child labour and poor working conditions, and wrote to The Guardian, prompting UK Parliament debate and eventually leading to labour reforms. She became politically active, winning her first Urban Council seat in 1963, and later served as vice-chairman from 1986 until her defeat in 1995, consistently receiving the highest votes. She was also the spokeswoman for the United Nations Association of Hong Kong, advocating for self-government. In 1966, she opposed a proposed 5-cent to 25-cent increase in Star Ferry fares, collecting over 20,000 signatories and flying to London to protest, which led to a hunger strike by So Sau-chung and eventually the Kowloon riots. She faced accusations of inciting the riots, dubbed the "Elliott riot," and was subjected to official inquiries. She campaigned against triad protection money and police corruption, reporting minibus rackets and corruption to various officials, including Governor Murray MacLehose and ICAC Director G. A. Harknett, and helped Mak Pui-yuen, who was victimised for reporting corruption. Her activism contributed to the establishment of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in 1974. In 1979, she co-founded the Association for the Promotion of Public Justice (APPJ) with Andrew Tu, which later established a Filipino Overseas Workers Group. She advocated for gay rights, urging decriminalisation as in the UK in 1967, though the government cited local opposition; homosexuality was decriminalised in Hong Kong in 1991. In 1980, after John MacLennan, a police inspector, was shot in his home during an investigation into homosexuality, she suggested he was persecuted for knowing too much and corresponded with MacLehose and other officials, leading to a Commission of Inquiry. In 1980, she was found under surveillance by the Standing Committee on Pressure Groups (SCOPG), but she remained unbothered, stating she had done nothing wrong. She was appointed to the HKSAR Basic Law Consultative Committee in 1985 and, when the Urban Council became an electoral college in 1985, she was elected to the Legislative Council in 1988, serving until 1995, during which she chaired the House Committee from 1991 to 1995 and remained the most popular legislator. In the lead-up to the 1997 handover, she supported a gradual pace of democratisation preferred by the Chinese government, opposing Governor Chris Patten's electoral reforms and criticising him as a hypocrite. In the March 1995 Urban Council election, she lost to Szeto Wah by 2,397 votes, and in the September 1995 Legislative Council election, she lost again in Kowloon East to Szeto Wah, supported by the pro-Beijing Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB). She was appointed to the Beijing-controlled Provisional Legislative Council from December 1996 to June 1998, serving on the Selection Committee responsible for electing the first Chief Executive. After the Provisional Legislative Council was dissolved in 1998, her political career ended. She stepped away from active politics but continued to comment on social issues and write critical articles. In 2002, she supported the enactment of the anti-subversion law under Basic Law Article 23, and in 2003, she publicly endorsed Regina Ip, who promoted the law, during the 1 July Protest with over 500,000 demonstrators. In 2013, she criticised widening income inequality and expressed sympathy for dock workers striking against billionaire Li Ka-shing's Hutchison Whampoa, marking her 100th birthday in June 2013. The Mu Kuang alumni established the Elsie Tu Education Fund in her honour. She died on 8 December 2015 at the age of 102 from pneumonia-related complications at Kwun Tong United Christian Hospital. All three former Chief Executives—Tung Chee-hwa, Donald Tsang, and Leung Chun-ying—were pallbearers at her funeral on 20 December, and her ashes were buried with those of her husband, Andrew Tu, at the Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan. Her father, John Hume, a grocer's assistant who fought in the First World War and was gassed, profoundly influenced her conscience and world-view, instilling in her a hatred of war and compassion for people, as well as a left-leaning perspective on religion, Marxism, and workers' rights. She married William Elliott, eight years her junior, and described the period as the lowest point in her life, eventually divorcing him in 1964. She later married Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei, who came to Hong Kong from Inner Mongolia in the 1950s, and they worked together at Mu Kuang English School, with Andrew teaching Chinese and Elliott teaching other Form 1 subjects. She believed Andrew's ideas reminded her of her father's values.

Elsie Tu's worldview was shaped by her father's influence, leading her in her youth to believe that "I could at least be good and useful in life"; her father died when she was in China. She married William Elliott, who was eight years her junior, and worked with the Plymouth Brethren missionary group in 1946. In 1947, she traveled to China with her husband, but grew increasingly disillusioned with his fundamentalism and their church, describing the period as "the lowest point in [her] life" and considering suicide. The couple separated during an abortive trip back to England, and she returned to Hong Kong alone, later divorcing him in 1964. In Hong Kong, she met her second husband, Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei, who had come from Inner Mongolia in the 1950s. They became working partners at the Mu Kuang English School, with Andrew teaching Chinese and Elliott teaching all other Form 1 subjects; despite cultural and language differences, Elsie found Andrew's ideas brought her back to her father's values. In 1985, 30 years after meeting, they married when Elsie was 71 and Andrew was 63, remaining married until Andrew died in 2001. Andrew was also a social activist and leader of the Chinese Alliance for Commemoration of the Sino-Japanese War Victims, which demands justice, reparations, and apologies for victims of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Tu authored two volumes of autobiography and other works; Colonial Hong Kong in the Eyes of Elsie Tu was published in 2003, and Shouting at the Mountain: A Hong Kong Story of Love and Commitment, co-written with Andrew Tu, was completed after his death in 2001 and published in 2005. She also completed the publication of her husband's autobiography of his childhood in Inner Mongolia, Camel Bells in the Windy Desert. In the 1960s, Tu was recognized as a champion fighting for the underprivileged and against corruption; Chief Executive Leung Chun-ying praised her "passion and devotion to Hong Kong and her tremendous contributions to social reform and development" after her death, and Chief Secretary Carrie Lam recalled meeting her during her university days, describing her as an exemplary champion of social justice who commanded respect. Founding chairman of the Democratic Party Martin Lee praised her as a pioneer in fighting for democracy, and other democrats such as Lau Chin-shek, Lee Wing-tat, Fred Li Wah-ming, and Frederick Fung acknowledged that their involvement in social activism was inspired or assisted by Elsie Tu. Tu received numerous honours, including the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Government Service in 1975, a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 1977 for her anti-corruption work, and the Grand Bauhinia Medal (GBM) in 1997 as one of the first recipients of the highest honour in the SAR award system. She also received honorary degrees: an honorary doctoral degree in Social Science from the University of Hong Kong in 1988, honorary doctoral degrees in Laws from the Hong Kong Polytechnic University and in Social Science from the Open Learning Institute of Hong Kong in 1994, and honorary doctoral degrees in Civil Law from both Armstrong College (later Newcastle University) and Durham University in 1996.
